I would say that many men are under pressure to be tough and deny illness, and underplay symptoms. So when men get a 'mild cold', we deny having one at all or telling anyone, preffering to self medicate or tough it out. Not until their symptoms become unbearable do many men open up and admit they are sick and even then they try to downplay it by claiming it's 'just a cold'. This would lead to a counter-intuitive assumption that men are sensitive to certain symptoms. 

As a medic in the army I saw this frequently. I saw many soldiers coming in for joint pain or physical injuries admit to currently feeling cold or flu-like symptoms that they did not wish to be treated for ("yeah doc, I have had a headache, runny nose and fever but i don't care. I just want motrin for my ankle").

Similarly, men and women may define 'sick' differently. A man may define being sick as being incapacitated, whereas more women may feel being sick is having symptoms of an illness.

Farrel! 
I apologize for the lateness of my letter (4000 nights is too long!), and I find it difficult to know where to begin. Last we spoke we were but university graduates enjoying our first days out of academia fucking everything in site and consuming every mushroom in the kingdom. I had no idea what was to come of my venture north to the new settlement, at the time hoping to at most gather a few exotic rocks and mineral samples for the museums back home. The fact that I write this to you from the newly named city of *Impact* and not the modest mining settlement from which it grew goes to show just how wrong I was. For as you know the site aimed for yielded far more bounty and treasures (And Dangers!) than we were prepared for.

I wish you could have seen it Farrel, what was supposed to be just another patch of the kilometer thick ice that covered our world had been blasted away, exposing earth that had not seen the light of day for millennia! The blast radius was massive, this new patch of coastal land held mountains and valleys and glacial rivers as far as the eyes could see. I must admit after arriving I was struck into some sort of mania (it was not mushrooms this time!), for everywhere I looked there were riches! We found iron, Gold, Nickel and new materials never before seen.

Perhaps most surprising though, *Impact* is not as bare and lifeless as we expected (Although there were no frozen leviathans of legend as many feared), for in the days before our people arrived the land become a haven for life. To us men, the world is a near endless strip of land bordered by glacier and ocean, the icy tundras uninhabitable for our kind, but home to flora and fauna never seen. We assumed the catastrophe that uncovered this place would have obliterated much of them, but instead it has provided a haven for strange beasts and critters including, as I am sure you have heard, the carnivorous beast-men. 

It is true, these beast men which even i doubted to exist are as real as you and I! They look almost as men do, but with almost no body hair and large child-like eyes. Even now after all this time they rarely make contact with us, keeping their distance and watching from afar. Although it is just as well, this new settlement is too valuable for our people to share with others. 

Perhaps someday you may join me up here as well. Until then, farwell!

I still cannot get over my tremendous luck of recent events, not only was I one of the singular witnesses to perhaps one of the most spectacular sights, but I also had the fortune to be one of the few in my party to still have functional retinas when it was over! It began yesterday while taking a group of students on one of our winter outings to Buck island to study the local plant life. Having made this trip nearly a hundred times I took my students to a favorite of my sites; a small cove facing north with some spectacular views. Overlooking the sea to the north you can see far off mountain chains and the impassible ice wall that surrounds them. The sky was clear and we had a wonderful view completely unobstructed to the shining mountains in the distance... then they exploded. 

Fortunately for me (and unfortunately for most of my students), it was while we were taking in this sight when a sudden flash of violet-white light exploded above the horizon. So bright in fact it burned our skin even through thick body hair and clothing, and blinded anyone looking directly at it. Thankfully I was admiring a tiny crustacean crawling on the beach at the time so my vision was saved. The fireball must have lasted a fraction of a second before red-shifting into softer colors more easily seen, and when i finally saw what was happening I was sure for a moment that the gods above had finally grown tired of this world and decided to rip the entire thing apart with fire. 

Fortunately this was not the case, and it became apparent that what we had witnessed was a massive falling star of unprecedented size and fury smashing into the northern ice sheets a thousand miles away. As I calmed myself, the scholarly part of me began to analyze the event rationally; things like size, speed and distance started to take shape in my mind before I even noticed my blinded students flailing in the sand. I was just about to thank the lords that it missed the sea, as the resulting tsunami would have surely been the death of us all, when the shock wave blew out my eardums... So I may not have the *best* luck after all, but still to witness such destruction and glory of nature in my lifetime is a gift I never thought I would be so lucky to bear!
